title: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures (as in Lima or Solen).

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: r(\theta, t) = t\,f(\theta) from the umbo; f(\theta) = \cos\theta gives coaxial circles

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: All that we are immediately concerned with is the simple fact that where a velocity, such as our rate of growth, varies with its direction,—varies that is to say as a function of the angular divergence from a certain axis,—then, in a certain simple case, we get lines of growth laid down as a system of coaxial circles,

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Lines of growth in bivalves”. Scope: lamellibranch and brachiopod shells with visible growth lines

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: r(\theta, t) = t\,f(\theta) from the umbo; f(\theta) = \cos\theta gives coaxial circles

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-16: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.77

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim connects visible curves to explicit geometric growth models. Existing shell media can resolve the major pattern and named form differences using routine morphometrics.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Digitize successive growth lines on bivalve and brachiopod shells, test whether they share an umbonal axis, and fit circular, elliptical and direction-dependent growth models. Directional increment rates should quantitatively generate the observed line family.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fine growth lines may be below scan resolution.

Environmental interruptions can perturb otherwise regular line families.

discriminating power: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.85
analysis feasibility: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Coaxial versus concentric growth lines are visually and numerically distinguishable, and the named genera are well represented by open photographs. The directional-growth interpretation is a further fit, but the geometric pattern itself can confirm or refute the main statement. Measuring curves on existing images is standard and does not require new specimens.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Digitize growth lines of bivalves and brachiopods, including Anomia, Lima and Solen, and test whether they are coaxial circles, ellipses or other coaxial curves through the umbo rather than concentric curves about a shifting center. A directional growth function is then fit to the family of curves; concentric lines, or no single coaxial family, refute the geometric claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Several directional functions can generate similar coaxial families, so the simplest-function clause is less sharp than the coaxial geometry.

Abraded umbones hide the point the curves should share.
